sentences.text: Shri Pushyamitra Bhargav, learned counsel for the petitioner.
Shri Abhishek Tugnawat, learned Government Advocate for the respondents / State.

The petitioner before this Court has filed this present petition being aggrieved by the order dated 24.08.2019 passed by the District Magistrate, Barwani under the provisions of National Security Act, 1980.
02.

The petitioner's contention is that he is running a firm in the name and style of "M/s Balmukund Mohanlal"
registered with the Food Department and on 05.08.2019, the officer of the Food Department conducted a raid at his premises and seized certain materials.
The material was forwarded for analysis and F.I.R. was also registered in the matter.
03. It has been further contended that thereafter, an order of detention has been passed on 24.08.2019 under the provisions of National Security Act, 1980.

It has been stated that only one case was registered against the father of the petitioner, Mohanlal i.e. Case No.33/2013 for the offence under Section 26(2)(ii) r/w section 52 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and a fine was imposed against his father on 31.07.2014.

The petitioner's contention is that on the basis of solitary incident / registration of a case under the Food Safety and Standard Act, 2006, the petitioner could not have been detained under the National Security Act, 1980.
04. Reliance has been placed upon a judgment delivered in the case of Rinku @ Kuldeep Shukla v/s The State of Madhya Pradesh & Others reported in 2015 (3) MPLJ 157.

entities.text: Rinku @ Kuldeep Shukla v/s The State of Madhya Pradesh & Others reported in 2015 (3) MPLJ 157
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The petitioner has stated that he is a trader.

He is neither proprietor nor partner of the firm M/s Balmukunt Mohanlal, and therefore, merely because some food articles were misbranded, he cannot be punished in the manner and method it has been done in the present case.

sentences.text:
A reply has been filed on behalf of respondents No.1 to 4 and it has been stated that a raid was conducted at the premises of the petitioner and samples of ghee, poha, vanaspati, palm oil and gud were seized from the premises of the petitioner and the materials were forwarded to the State Examination Laboratory.
06.
The respondents have also stated that they have registered a F.I.R. for the offences under Sections 272, 273, 420 of the Indian Penal Code r/w Section 3 and 4 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955.
The respondents have stated that keeping in view the misbranded and adulterated food articles, they have rightly passed an order under the National Security Act, 1980.

07. Heard learned counsel for the parties at length and perused the record.
08.
This Court has carefully gone through the writ petition as well as the reply filed by the respondents.

Undisputedly, there is no other case registered against the petitioner except for the case registered at Police Station - Sendhwa City at Crime No.0255/2019 for the offences under Sections 272, 273, 420 r/w section 3 and 4 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955.
The adulterated food items were recovered from the premises where the petitioner was found and in those circumstances, he has been detained under the National Security Act, 1980.

09. A Division Bench of this Court in the case of Sudeep Jain v/s The State of Madhya Pradesh &
Others (W.P. No.21768/2019)

entities.text:
Sudeep Jain v/s The State of Madhya Pradesh &
Others (W.P. No.21768/2019)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: has dealt with the similar controversy, wherein Sandeep Jain, the petitioner therein was arrested for allegedly manufacturing adulterated ghee and mawa at his residence.

Paragraph - 4 to 21 of the aforesaid judgment reads as under :-
"4.
The impugned order is Annexure P/1 at page 22 and 23 of the petition.
The order has been passed, avowedly on the ground of preventing the Petitioner from acting in a manner prejudicial to public order.
Undisputedly, the impugned order does not specify the period of detention.
The consistent opinion of the Supreme Court is that the non-mention of the specific period of detention is by itself not fatal to proceedings under the law of preventive detention.

In 1951, a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court while examining the ambit and scope of section 12 of the "Preventive Detention Act, 1950", held that the Act does not require the period of detention to be mentioned1.

In Suna Ullah Butt's case, a three judge bench of the Supreme Court while examining the scope of section 12 and 13 of the "Jammu and Kashmir Preventive Detention Act, 1964" held "The second contention of Mr Om Prakash relates to the fact that the period for which the petitioner was to be detained has not been mentioned in the order of the State Government, dated March 3, 1972,
confirming the detention order.

entities.text: Jammu and Kashmir Preventive Detention Act, 1964
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: It is urged that the failure of the State Government to specify the period of detention introduces an infirmity in the detention of the petitioner.
This contention, in our opinion, is without any force........
There is nothing in the section which enjoins upon the Government to specify the period of detention also while confirming the detention order.

The concluding words of subsection (1) of Section 12, according to which the Government may continue the detention of the person concerned for such period as it thinks fit, pertain to and embody the Balmukund Garg vs Home Department on 2 December, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34392169/
2 consequence of the confirmation of the detention order"2.
5.
However, a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court in Gurbux Anandram Bhiryani's case held otherwise.

In a brief order, the Supreme Court while examining an in pari materia provision in the "Maharashtra Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Slumlords, Bootleggers and Drug Offenders Act, 1981" held "The order is bad on another ground, namely, the period of detention has not been indicated by the detaining authority.

entities.text: Maharashtra Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Slumlords, Bootleggers and Drug Offenders Act, 1981
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The scheme of this Act differs from the provisions contained in similar Acts by not prescribing a period of detention but as Section 3 of the Act indicates, there is an initial period of detention which can extend up to three months and that can be extended for periods of three months at a time.
It was open to the detaining authority to detain the detenu even for a period of lesser duration than three months.
That necessitated the period of detention to be specified and unless that was indicated in the order, the order would also be vitiated"3.

It is relevant to mention here that the two judge bench, did not refer to the judgements of the Constitution Bench in Ujagar Singh's case and that of the three-judge bench in Suna Ullah Butt's case passed earlier, which held to the contrary.

6. This order passed by the two-judge bench of the Supreme Court was expressly overruled by a three- judge bench of the Supreme Court in T.Devaki's case where the Supreme Court once again reiterated the position in Ujagar Singh and Suna Ullah Butt's case.
The Court held "The Act nowhere requires the detaining authority to specify the period for which the detenu is required to be detained.

The expression "the State Government are satisfied that it is necessary so to do, they may, by order in writing direct that during such period as may be specified in the order" occurring in sub- section (2) of Section 3 relates to the period for which the order of delegation issued by the State Government is to remain in force and it has no relevance to the period of detention"4.
7.

As recently as 2018, the view expressed in T. Devaki's case was once again considered and approved of by another three-judge bench of the Supreme Court where it held "In T. Devaki v. State of T.N. [T. Devaki v. State of T.N., (1990) 2 SCC 456 :
1990 SCC (Cri) 348] , a Bench of this Court has held that since the legislation does not require the detaining authority to specify the period for which a detenu is required to be detained, the order of detention is not rendered invalid or illegal in the absence of such specification.....

entities.text:
T. Devaki v. State of T.N. [T. Devaki v. State of T.N., (1990) 2 SCC 456 :
1990 SCC (Cri) 348
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the circumstances, the High Court was not justified in quashing the order of detention on the basis that no period of detention was provided in the order.

The High Court has proceeded on the basis of the decision of this Court in Bhiryani [Commr. of Police v. Gurbux Anandram Bhiryani, 1988 Supp SCC 568 : 1988 SCC (Cri) 914] which is no longer good law in view of the subsequent decision of a larger Bench in Devaki [T. Devaki v. State of T.N., (1990) 2 SCC 456 : 1990 SCC (Cri) 348]...."5.
Balmukund Garg vs Home Department on 2 December, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34392169/
3 8.

entities.text: Bhiryani [Commr. of Police v. Gurbux Anandram Bhiryani, 1988 Supp SCC 568 : 1988 SCC (Cri) 914]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Devaki [T. Devaki v. State of T.N., (1990) 2 SCC 456 : 1990 SCC (Cri) 348]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Thus, on the basis of the judgements of the Supreme Court mentioned hereinabove, this Court holds that an order of detention under the NSA is not vitiated, merely because it does not specify the period of detention, as there is no provision in the NSA mandating such a requirement.

The phrase "period specified" in the proviso to section 3(3) of the NSA is the period of subsistence of the authority delegated on the District Magistrate or the Commissioner of Police, and the same has received sufficient elucidation by this Court in Writ Petition No. 17609/2019 (Chotu@Suyash Chaubey Vs. Union of India and Others) and therefore, we do not find the need to dwell on this point.

entities.text: Chotu@Suyash Chaubey Vs. Union of India and Others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: However, such an omission is relevant as it discloses a non-application of mind on the part of the authority.
In this regard this Court feels that the obiter dicta in Gurbux Anandram Bhiriyani's case is relevant.

Though the said judgement has been overruled on the point of law, the observation of the Supreme Court that, even though, the period of detention is three months, nothing prevents the authority from detaining the detenu for a shorter period, assumes relevance while assessing the application of mind on the part of the detaining authority.

Under the circumstance, where the order mentions the period of detention, it reflects that the detaining authority has considered the sum totality of the circumstances against the detenu and then arrived at a subjective satisfaction with regard to the period, for which the detenu is required to be detained.
The absence of the period of detention is reflective of the authority having mechanically proceeded is passing the order by signing on a cyclostyled paper.
Thus, the absence of the period of detention when seen in conjunction with the other reasons given hereinafter, renders the impugned order bad in law.

9. The Ld. Counsel for the Petitioner has submitted that the grounds of detention served upon him inform him that he has a right to represent to the State Government and that he has a right to audience before the Advisory Board to present his case.

It is the case of the Petitioner, that the said order does not inform his of his right to make a representation to the detaining authority or to the Central Government, and the failure to inform his thus, vitiates and renders the impugned order bad in law.

In order to assess the correctness of this contention, it would be essential to briefly examine Ss. 3(4), 3(5), 8 and 14 of the NSA and section 21 of the General Clause Act, 1897 (hereinafter referred to as the "GCA").
10.
The right of the detenu to represent to the authorities under the NSA is wide.
In the absence of any restriction under the NSA, the detenu has a right to make a representation to the District Magistrate itself, who is the detaining authority.

There is a strong rationale in support of this arrangement as the order of detention passed by the District Magistrate is based upon the report of the police and therefore it follows, that at the time of passing the order of detention, the District Magistrate had only the opinion of the police before him.

Under the circumstances, the DM may well change his opinion with regard to the necessity to detain the detenu once he is apprised of the case from the side of the detenu and may revoke the order of detention.
11. Section 3(4) inter alia provides that the order of detention shall remain in force for twelve days unless, approved by the State Government.

Thus, immediately after passing the order of detention,
the detenu has to be informed that he has the right to make a representation to the State Government for the revocation of his detention.
Section 3(5) mandates that the Central Government be informed within seven days of the approval being granted by the State Government.
Section 8 provides for the supply of the grounds of detention to the detenu so that he may prefer a representation to the appropriate Government.
Section 21 of the GCA provides that an authority which can pass an order, has the right to add, amend, vary or rescind the order.

Balmukund Garg vs Home Department on 2 December, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34392169/
4 12.

entities.text: Balmukund Garg vs Home Department on 2 December, 2019 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: From a conjoint reading of the provisions aforementioned, it follows that the detenu has to be informed about his right to represent to the State Government, Central Government and to the Advisory Board.
Most importantly in the light of section 21 of the GCA, the District Magistrate must inform the detenu of his right to make a representation to the District Magistrate itself.

This right to represent to the detaining authority itself was examined by the Supreme Court in Santosh Shankar Acharya's case where the Court examined the right of a detenu to make a representation to the detaining authority and the effect of non-communication to the detenu of the said right, under the "Maharashtra Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Slumlords, Bootleggers, Drug-Offenders and Dangerous Persons Act, 1981".

entities.text: Maharashtra Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Slumlords, Bootleggers, Drug-Offenders and Dangerous Persons Act, 1981
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: In that case, an argument was put forth that the detaining authority became functus officio once he passed the order of detention.
It was also contended that it was the State Government which was the authority to decide the representation of the detenu.
Here, it would be essential to state that the provisions of the Maharashtra Act and the NSA are largely in pari materia.

Rejecting the contention, the Supreme Court held that in view of section 21 of the Bombay General Clauses Act (which is similar to section 21 of the General Clauses Act), the detaining authority has the power to entertain the representation of the detenu till the order of detention was approved by the State Government.

Thereafter, the Supreme Court examined the non-communication to the detenu, his right to represent to the detaining authority in the following words, "...This being the position, noncommunication of the fact to the detenu that he could make a representation to the detaining authority so long as the order of detention has not been approved by the State Government in a case where an order of detention is issued by an officer other than the State Government under sub-section (2) of section 3of the Maharashtra Act would constitute an infraction of a valuable right of the detenu under Article 22(5) of the Constitution..."6 13.
Earlier, in the year 1995, a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court also held as above in the case of Kamlesh Kumar Ishwardas Patel.

The Court held that "Article 22(5) must therefore, be construed to mean that the person detained has a right to make a representation against the order of detention which can be made not only to the Advisory Board but also to the detaining authority, i.e.,
the authority that has made the order of detention or the order for the continuance of such detention, which is competent to give immediate relief by revoking the said order as well as to any other authority which is competent under law to revoke the order for detention and thereby give relief to the person detained.

The right to make a representation carries within it a corresponding obligation on the authority making the order of detention to inform the person detained of his right to make a representation against the order of detention to the authorities who are required to consider such an application"7.
Thus, in the present case, the grounds of detention only inform the Petitioner with regard to his right to make a representation against the order of detention to the State Government.
It does no reflect that the Petitioner was also informed that he had the right to make a representation to detaining authority also.
Under the circumstances, the impugned order stands vitiated and is liable to be quashed.
14. The grounds of detention are of even date and is Annexure P/2 to the petition at page 24 to 25.

The satisfaction of the District Magistrate for detaining the Petitioner under the NSA is reflected in paragraph 2 of the grounds which reads thus;"               
   !            !                ,
Magistrate arrives at the finding that in the case against the Petitioner, the report of the analyst has Balmukund Garg vs Home Department on 2 December, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34392169/
5 established that seized food material is of sub-standard quality.

The District Magistrate further held that the Petitioner is playing with the health of the general public and in order to deter others from doing the same, it is necessary to act is the most stringent manner.

In the same paragraph, the District Magistrate arrives at the finding that "...              
 1                  ! /

Here, the District Magistrate opines that the activities of the Petitioner has resulted in grave danger to public health due to which there is great resentment against the Petitioner in the mind of the public on account of which there is grave danger to public order.

In another place in the same paragraph, the District Magistrate opines "  78          "   or that on account of the activity of the Petitioner, there is a health hazard posed to human life.
15.

Along with the grounds of detention, the criminal record of the Petitioner is annexed (page 26)
which shows that there is only one criminal case that exists against the Petitioner which is Crime No. 531/19 which has been registered by the police in the present case.

The grounds of detention also refer to a case against the Petitioner of the year 2015 where the Petitioner was fined rupees four thousand for having in his possession for sale, milk that was found to be sub-standard.
16. The report of the public analyst establishes that the samples of ghee and mawa taken from the Petitioner were sub-standard.
The report does not establish that sample tested was found to be hazardous to human health upon consumption.

To have a better understanding of the effect of the Petitioner's act, it would be essential to refer to certain provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the "FSSA").

The term "sub-standard" is defined in section 3(1)(zx) of the FSSA as "an article of food shall be deemed to be sub-standard if it does not meet the specified standards but not so as to render the article of food unsafe;".
The FSSA also defines the term "unsafe food" in section 3(1)(zz) as "means an article of food whose nature, substance or quality is so affected as to render it injurious to health".

Under the circumstances, the undisputed case of the State is that the food articles were only sub-standard as per the analyst report, or in other words, the standards that have been specified under the FSSA for ghee and mawa were not met by the samples taken from the Petitioner.
By no stretch of imagination can the samples taken from the Petitioner be deemed to be injurious to health, as per the definition of sub-standard given in the FSSA.
17. The impugned order smacks of gross non- application of mind.
The District Magistrate has acted in the most cavalier manner in passing the impugned order of detention.
She has repeatedly held in the grounds of detention that the act of the Petitioner is hazardous to public health and wellbeing as he was selling food material that was unsafe.
It is apparent that the District Magistrate has not even cared to assess the import of the term "sub- standard" and its distinction from "unsafe food" by looking into the FSSA.

Had she done so, she would have realised that (a) food, which according to the report of the analyst is "sub-standard", is not food that is dangerous or deleterious for human consumption as against "unsafe food", which is.

(b) the FSSA does not even provide for the punishment of imprisonment for the sale of "sub-standard" food and makes the act punishable only with fine as is provided under section 51 of the FSSA which reads "Any person who whether by himself or by any other person on his behalf manufactures for sale or stores or sells Balmukund Garg vs Home Department on 2 December, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34392169/
6 or distributes or imports any article of food for human consumption which is sub-standard, shall be liable to a penalty which may extend to five lakh rupees"
18.
Thus, the impugned order is bad in law as, for the reason given hereinabove, complete lack of application of mind is reflected on the part of the District Magistrate in passing the order.

The District Magistrate has also failed to appreciate that criminal record of the Petitioner, given by the police reflects that besides the FIR mentioned hereinabove, no other criminal case exists against the Petitioner.

Even assuming that the detention of the Petitioner was otherwise justifiable, one singular offence registered by the police is inadequate to resort to the draconian provisions of the NSA to deprive a citizen's liberty.

In this regard, it would be relevant to refer to the opinion of the Supreme Court in a case of preventive detention based upon a single case under the provisions of the IPC,
where the Supreme Court held that ".....An individual incident under the Penal Code, however heinous, is insufficient to make out a case for issuance of an order of preventive detention"8.
19.

The District Magistrate failed to appreciate the principal of law that the general law shall not nullify the provisions of the special law as is enshrined in the maxim "generalia specialibus non derogant".
Where there exists a special statute to deal with a particular situation, then the resort to preventive detention under the NSA (the general law) is uncalled for.

Where the legislative wisdom reflected in a special statute like the FSSA does not provide for the imprisonment of a person whose act is at conflict with certain provisions of the FSSA, then subjecting such person to preventive detention under the NSA, for the same act, is not merely an abuse of process but a glaring instance of malicious exercise of executive discretion and the same has to be derided in the strongest terms.
In this regard, the opinion of the Supreme Court is extremely relevant where it held "Preventive detention is, by nature, repugnant to democratic ideas and an anathema to the rule of law.
No such law exists in the USA and in England (except during war time).

Since, however, Article 22(3)(b) of the Constitution of India permits preventive detention, we cannot hold it illegal but we must confine the power of preventive detention within very narrow limits, otherwise we will be taking away the great right to liberty guaranteed by Article 21 of the Constitution of India which was won after long,
arduous and historic struggles.

It follows, therefore, that if the ordinary law of the land (the Penal Code and other penal statutes) can deal with a situation, recourse to a preventive detention law will be illegal"9.
20.
The FSSA is a regulatory statute with certain penal provisions.
Regulatory Statutes are laws that are made by the legislature to regulate the conduct of certain human activities.

Such statutes may provide for certain penal provisions where the legislature in its wisdom, is of the opinion that certain acts need to be prevented and in order to ensure compliance, sanctions in the form of imprisonment may be provided.
Actions which are violative of such special laws must be dealt with under the provisions of those laws.

Action on the part of the State to deter the same by resorting to preventive detention, where the special statute does not even provide for imprisonment for the said act is deplorable and worthy of derision in the strongest terms.

It would also be an instance of the executive exceeding the will of the legislature and such resort to preventive detention, gravely impinges upon the fundamental right to life itself of a person so proceeded against.

Where the State resorts to proceedings under the NSA against individuals, whose actions are violations under regulatory statutes, and whose liberty is infringed by the State and its functionaries by a perverse Balmukund Garg vs Home Department on 2 December, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34392169/
7 and contorted interpretation of the phrase "public order", the same shall attract severe indictment of the State and the officers responsible for such malicious exercise of executive discretion.

21. In the present case, the reasoning given by the District Magistrate for arriving at the opinion that the Petitioner is a threat to public order, only because the sample of ghee and mawa seized tested out to be sub- standard, is ludicrous and downright preposterous, a result of contorted reasoning.

Thus, the impugned order passed by the District Magistrate is violative of the fundamental right of the Petitioner under Article 21 of the Constitution and has resulted in the illegal detention of the Petitioner and so, the same is quashed.
However, as the Petitioner has not made a prayer for the award of deterrent compensation, no such order is being passed.

However, the Court preserves the right of the Petitioner to approach the State or National Human Rights Commission for such relief if he so desires."
10.
In the present case also, there is no report brought to the notice of this Court, which establishes that the samples tested, were found to be hazardous for health upon human consumption.

Otherwise also, on the basis of registration of a single case against the petitioner from the premises of a firm of which he is not a partner or proprietor, the order under the National Security Act, 1980 has been passed.
11. In the considered opinion of this Court, the impugned order dated 24.08.2019 deserves to be quashed and is accordingly, quashed.
The Writ Petition stands allowed.
Certified copy, as per rules.

(S.C. SHARMA) (SHAILENDRA SHUKLA)
